cards.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus, is writing to the believers in Rome (Romans 1:1, 7). He just told them they're not under law but under grace (Romans 6:15). Now he turns to his brothers who know the law and asks them how long the law gets a say over a person.

cards.question: How long does Paul say the law has authority over a man?

answers.text: Only as long as he lives
Only as long as he lives in Israel

cards.text: Then Paul gives a picture every grown-up can follow: marriage. A married woman is bound by law to her husband as long as he lives.

cards.question: In Paul's marriage picture, if the husband dies, the woman is still bound by the law of marriage.

cards.text: Paul spells it out. If she's joined to another man while her husband is still alive, she's called an adulteress.

cards.question: But if her husband dies and she marries another man, Paul says she is not an ___.

cards.text: Now Paul brings the picture home. You also died to the law, he says, through the body of Christ.

cards.question: Paul says the believers died to the law so they could belong to someone new. Who?

answers.text: Him who was raised from the dead
The elders of the church in Jerusalem
The teachers who know the law best

cards.question: Paul says the point of belonging to the risen Christ is that we might bear ___ to God.

cards.text: Then Paul looks back at the old days, when we lived according to the flesh. Sinful passions were at work in our bodies, which is like a batch burning in the oven while everybody ignores the timer going off.

cards.question: Paul says those sinful passions at work in our bodies were aroused by the ___.
Paul says those sinful passions were bearing fruit for death.

cards.text: But now, Paul says, we've died to what bound us and been released from the law. Friend, I spent YEARS in the back of a junk drawer waiting to feel RELEASED.

cards.question: Now that they're released from the law, how does Paul say believers serve?

answers.text: In the new way of the Spirit
In the old way of the written code
In the strict way of the elders

cards.text: Paul can see the next question coming like a group chat that only read half the text. If we've been released from the law, does that mean the law is sin?

cards.question: Paul says the law is sin.

cards.text: Then Paul says, "Indeed, I would not have been mindful of sin if not for the law." The law is what pointed his sin out to him.

cards.question: Paul gives one example of a sin he wouldn't have been aware of if the law hadn't named it. Which one?

cards.text: Then Paul says sin seized its opportunity through the commandment. It's like a sign that says DO NOT TOUCH, and suddenly your hand is hovering there like it's got a mind of its own.

cards.question: Paul says sin, through the commandment, produced in him every kind of ___ desire.
Paul says that apart from the law, sin is dead.

cards.text: Then Paul says, "Once I was alive apart from the law; but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life and I died."

cards.question: What does Paul discover about the commandment that was meant to bring life?

answers.text: It was only for the priests

cards.text: Paul explains how, and there's that line again. Sin seized its opportunity through the commandment.

cards.question: What does Paul say sin did to him through the commandment before it put him to death?

cards.text: So is the commandment the bad guy here? Sin is the one that used it, and believe me, I know what it's like getting blamed for a crooked cookie when somebody else did the pressing.

cards.question: So then, Paul says the law is ___.

cards.text: One last question from Paul. Did that which is good become death to him? Certainly not, he says.

cards.question: So why does Paul say sin produced death in him through something good?

answers.text: So sin would be exposed as sin
So the law would look stronger
So Paul would stop reading it

cards.question: Paul says that through the commandment, sin might become utterly sinful.

findings.problem: The card says Paul 'just told them they're not under law but under grace' and cites Romans 6:15. In 6:15 that phrase sits inside a question ('Shall we sin because we are not under law but under grace?'). Paul states it in Romans 6:14, so the reference doesn't match what the card says he told them.

rule.text: Noticing. What he points out must be true.

findings.problem: The right answer, 'Him who was raised from the dead,' is in Bible wording. The two wrong answers are plain modern phrasing ('The elders of the church in Jerusalem,' 'The teachers who know the law best'), so the right answer stands out. 'The teachers who know the law best' is also not a real Bible detail, which a who question needs.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The blank asks the baker to guess the wording 'bear fruit to God.' 'Bear burdens' is just as believable, and nothing on the earlier cards lets the baker reason their way to 'fruit.' It tests wording the baker hasn't seen, not meaning.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The comparison doesn't match the core action. Verse 5 is about sinful passions at work and bearing fruit for death. The joke is about ignoring a timer, which is a warning being ignored. That action isn't in the verse, so the image doesn't click and the joke doesn't land.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The joke is muddled. Paul 'can see the next question coming like a group chat that only read half the text' compares Paul seeing a question to a group chat, and a group chat doesn't read. A stranger would say 'huh?'

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: The card ties Paul's question to being released from the law ('If we've been released from the law, does that mean the law is sin?'). Romans 7:7 only asks 'What then shall we say? Is the law sin?' and doesn't say what the question follows from.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The wrong answers aren't believable. 'It actually brought riches' is silly in context, and 'It was only for the priests' isn't the same kind of thing as the other two answers, which both say what the commandment brought.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The card cites Romans 7:11-12 but tells nothing from 7:12. 'Sin is the one that used it' comes from 7:11. What 7:12 says, that the law is holy, is told only on the next choice card.

rule.text: Cite exactly what the card uses. Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The joke adds a new moment to his backstory: being blamed in the Millers' kitchen for a crooked cookie when somebody else did the pressing. In the backstory, the trouble was his own worn edges, and Mother Miller never complained. The joke shifts the blame onto someone else and reads like an old grievance.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'finished' can be argued from the passage. Verses 4 and 6 say believers died to the law and were released from it, so a baker could argue the law is finished.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'So Paul would stop reading it' is silly and not believable as a reason for verse 13.

rule.text: For why and meaning questions, wrong answers only need to be believable.

findings.problem: Most story cards are flat retelling with no Papa Dorin voice (stop 1 cards 1, 5 and 7; stop 2 cards 3, 8, 10 and 14). The jokes that are there don't land: stop 1 card 10 and stop 2 card 1 are broken, and stop 1 card 13 ('waiting to feel RELEASED') reads like a nice dad being pleasant.

rule.text: When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
